title: Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president?
gist: Chatham House argues Saddam Haftar has consolidated his position as heir to Khalifa Haftar and, buoyed by a US-led (Massad Boulos) Haftar-Dabaiba power-sharing channel that gives the LAAF parity with the GNU, is grabbing institutions (House speaker, Central Bank governor, Turkey maritime MoU) in a push for the presidency. Entrenched western opposition and the Dabaibas' refusal to make him president mean his bid raises the risk of renewed conflict.

insights.claim: Khalifa Haftar's 2025 appointment of his son Saddam Haftar as LAAF deputy general commander sealed Saddam as heir apparent, easing fears that the family-run Libyan Arab Armed Forces would fragment after the 83-year-old commander.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reduced eastern Libya succession-fragmentation risk; Saddam is now the counterparty for anyone dealing with the east.
insights.quote: Khalifa’s appointment of Saddam as deputy general commander in August 2025 sealed his position as heir apparent.

insights.claim: After the LAAF's failed 2020 assault on Tripoli, Khalifa Haftar restructured the force, putting land forces under Saddam Haftar and security units under Khaled Haftar.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Military control in eastern Libya is concentrated in the Haftar sons, not institutions.
insights.locator: Their rise became clearer after the failure

insights.claim: Saddam Haftar's power rests not only on his military command but also on alleged growing influence, via proxies, over eastern Libya's oil and gas and banking sectors.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Eastern Libyan hydrocarbon output and revenue flows are increasingly tied to one individual's political ambitions.
insights.quote: his alleged increasing influence via proxies over the oil and gas and banking sectors in eastern Libya
insights.locator: Saddam has become the most powerful of the sons

insights.claim: Belgassim Haftar built the family's political networks and since 2023 has headed the Libyan Development and Reconstruction Programme created after the Derna floods, giving the Haftars a development narrative.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reconstruction spending in the east is a Haftar-controlled channel for patronage and legitimacy.

insights.claim: The US unification push led by Massad Boulos seeks a deal between Libya's two ruling families, the Haftars in the east and the Dabaibas running the Tripoli GNU, reportedly with Saddam Haftar joining the Presidency Council while the Dabaibas keep the prime minister post.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A US-brokered power-sharing deal is the main path to a unified Libyan government; watch for its terms leaking.

insights.claim: The US plan broke with the prior formula of negotiating between Libya's House of Representatives and High State Council, and its first output was a Haftar-Dabaiba budget spending deal in April 2026.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Libyan fiscal outcomes are now set by elite bargains between two families, not by institutions.

insights.claim: The UN Mission adapted to the US format through a '4+4' committee of GNU, LAAF, House of Representatives and High State Council representatives, which agreed a roadmap for national elections in August 2026.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: An elections roadmap exists on paper, but the article argues outcomes would be contested.

insights.claim: The shift of Libyan negotiations to an LAAF-GNU channel matters more than any agreement's content because it puts Saddam Haftar's LAAF General Command on formal parity with the internationally recognized GNU.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: International legitimacy is moving toward the eastern command, a structural gain for Saddam.
insights.quote: is more significant than the content of the agreement. It officially places Saddam’s LAAF General Command as a negotiating party with parity with the internationally recognized GNU

insights.claim: The October 2026 ousting of the longtime House of Representatives speaker and his replacement with a pro-LAAF figure is widely understood to have been orchestrated by Saddam Haftar.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Saddam now likely controls Libya's eastern legislature, enabling him to push ratifications that serve his bid.

insights.claim: Libya's House of Representatives moved to ratify a contested memorandum with Turkey recognizing drilling rights in the eastern Mediterranean, reportedly at Saddam Haftar's push to win Ankara's backing for his presidential bid, angering Egypt and European states.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Eastern Mediterranean maritime and drilling disputes with Egypt and Europe could sharpen; Turkey gains leverage in Libya.
insights.locator: Shortly after, the House of Representatives moved

insights.claim: On 26 October 2026 the Central Bank of Libya governor was replaced, reportedly via a private Haftar-Dabaiba agreement, putting control of foreign-currency and dinar distribution under the two families' bargain.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Central bank leadership changes affect FX allocation and oil-revenue distribution; watch for policy shifts on dinar and hard-currency access.

insights.claim: Influential international actors increasingly see Saddam Haftar as the partner of preference because he appears able to get things done and keep order, compared with contested power in western Libya.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Foreign backing is consolidating behind the east, raising odds of a Saddam-centred settlement or confrontation.

themes.theme: Rising conflict risk in western Libya

insights.claim: Opposition to Saddam Haftar remains strong in western Libya, especially in Misrata, worsened by the August 2026 discovery of an allegedly LAAF-linked sleeper cell accused of planning to damage oil and gas infrastructure in Zawiya.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Sabotage risk to western Libyan energy infrastructure is a live tail risk for Libyan output.
insights.locator: But opposition to – and mistrust of

insights.claim: The Dabaiba family may cut deals to keep a modus vivendi with Saddam Haftar but is highly unlikely to sign a deal making him president, as shown by the lack of a deal despite months of intensive US mediation by Massad Boulos.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Discount headlines of an imminent unified-government deal; partial technical deals are more likely than a presidency settlement.
insights.quote: it is highly unlikely to sign a deal making Saddam president

insights.claim: Libyan elections would not settle power: according to a security-sector source, Saddam Haftar would reject a loss and his opponents would reject his win, so his continued presidential push raises the risk of renewed conflict.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat Libyan election milestones as conflict-risk events, not stabilizers; watch Tripoli security and oil-export disruption.
insights.quote: even if there were elections, Saddam would not accept the results if he loses, and his opponents would not accept the results if he wins

insights.claim: Western Libyan actors want military reunification talks separated from political reunification because no meaningful guarantees can reassure them that Saddam Haftar would share power.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Military-reunification progress (e.g. talks held in Turkey) may not translate into political unity.
insights.locator: Many doubt that Saddam is willing

insights.claim: Saddam Haftar's allies in Tripoli are reportedly preparing the ground for his arrival, while his opponents, who prefer the messy status quo to a Saddam-dominated order, see their options narrowing as international support for him builds.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Escalation risk in the capital is rising; a forced entry into Tripoli would be a major Libya risk event.
insights.locator: Saddam is now central to any political effort
